subject: mathematics
question_text: Show that 4ⁿ − 3n − 1 is divisible by 9, ∀ n ∈ N.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.29, chapter 4 MATHEMATICAL INDUCTION, Short Answer question 7(iii). Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The split gives one mark to each of the four moves an induction proof is marked on — the base case, the hypothesis, the inductive step and the closing appeal to the principle — and leaves the opening statement step unmarked, matching every other card in this chapter. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B prints eight short answers of which the student writes any six, each worth 4 marks, and Mathematical Induction supplies one of them on almost every paper. A note on the base case: at n = 1 the expression is 0, and 0 = 9 × 0 is divisible by 9, so S(1) is true and the card says so in full rather than quietly starting at n = 2. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this by induction — how you write divisibility as an equation, and what you substitute in the third step.

steps.label: Write the statement
steps.margin_note: Unmarked setup at 4 marks, but never skip it — divisibility is written as an EQUATION, equal to 9 times an integer. Without that line there is nothing to substitute later.

recall.must_convey: That 'divisible by 9' is written as an equation: the expression equals 9q for some integer q.
accept: write it as four to the n minus three n minus one equals nine q where q is an integer
divisible by nine means it equals nine times some integer
set the expression equal to nine q with q an integer
nine q ki equal ga rastam q integer
reject: let s of n be the statement

steps.why: You cannot do algebra with the word 'divisible'. Turning it into = 9q is what lets Step 3 replace 4ᵏ by something written in terms of q.
common_mistakes: Leaving the statement in words, so Step 3 has nothing to use.
Forgetting to say q is an integer, which is the whole content of divisibility.
steps.memory_tip: Divisibility becomes = 9q with q an integer. That one line is what Step 3 substitutes.

steps.label: Check S(1)
steps.margin_note: One mark. The value at n = 1 is 0, and 0 is a multiple of 9 — write that out, do not skip past it.

recall.must_convey: That at n = 1 the expression is 0, and 0 equals 9 times 0, so it is divisible by 9 and S(1) is true.
accept: four minus three minus one is zero and zero is nine times zero so it is divisible
at n equals one you get zero which is a multiple of nine
the first case gives zero and zero counts as divisible by nine
n equals one ki zero vasthundi adi nine multiple

steps.why: Zero is a multiple of every number, so S(1) is genuinely true and the proof may start at n = 1. The first non-zero case, n = 2, gives 16 − 6 − 1 = 9, which is a useful check that the expression was copied correctly.
common_mistakes: Saying 0 is not divisible by 9 and starting the proof at n = 2 without being asked to.
Mishandling the −1 and getting 1 instead of 0.
steps.memory_tip: At n = 1 the value is 0, and 0 = 9 × 0. Check n = 2 as well: 16 − 6 − 1 = 9.

steps.label: Assume S(k) is true
steps.margin_note: One mark. Assume it for k, then REARRANGE to make 4ᵏ the subject — that rearranged line is what Step 3 substitutes.
lines: Step 2 — assume S(k) is true, k ∈ N

recall.must_convey: That S(k) is assumed as 4ᵏ − 3k − 1 = 9q, and rearranged to give 4ᵏ = 9q + 3k + 1.
accept: assume it for k so four to the k minus three k minus one is nine q and make four to the k the subject
rearrange the assumption to get four to the k equals nine q plus three k plus one
suppose s of k holds then write the power in terms of q
k ki assume chesi four power k ni subject ga rastam
reject: take it as true for k

steps.why: Step 3 meets 4ᵏ⁺¹, which is 4 × 4ᵏ. Having 4ᵏ already written in terms of q is what makes that substitution possible.
common_mistakes: Assuming the statement for all k rather than one k.
Sign slip when moving −3k − 1 across, giving 4ᵏ = 9q − 3k − 1.
steps.memory_tip: Rearrange to make 4ᵏ the SUBJECT: 4ᵏ = 9q + 3k + 1. Step 3 puts that straight in.

steps.label: Show S(k+1) follows
steps.margin_note: One mark, and the longest step on the page. Split 4ᵏ⁺¹ as 4·4ᵏ, substitute (1), and gather until 9 comes out as a factor.

recall.must_convey: That 4ᵏ⁺¹ is written as 4·4ᵏ, the rearranged assumption is substituted, and everything collects into 9(4q + k) — a multiple of 9 because the bracket is an integer.
accept: write four to the k plus one as four times four to the k then substitute and it comes to nine into four q plus k
substitute the assumption and take nine out as a factor
the constants cancel and twelve k minus three k leaves nine k
substitute chesi nine common teeste integer migulutundi
reject: I show s of k plus one
heard_as: four to the k plus one

steps.why: The two constants +4 and −4 cancel, and 12k − 3k leaves 9k. Both surviving terms, 36q and 9k, carry a factor 9 — that is why the expression works.
common_mistakes: Stopping at 9(…) without saying the bracket is an integer, which is what divisibility requires.
steps.memory_tip: Split 4ᵏ⁺¹ as 4·4ᵏ, substitute, and the +4 and −4 cancel: 36q + 9k = 9(4q + k).

steps.label: Conclude by P.M.I
steps.margin_note: The last mark is for naming the principle. One sentence, one full mark.
lines: Hence, by the principle of finite

recall.must_convey: That S(1) is true and S(k) implies S(k+1), so by the principle of mathematical induction the expression is divisible by 9 for every natural number n.
accept: since the first case is true and each case gives the next by p m i it is true for all n
hence by the principle of mathematical induction it is divisible by nine for every natural number
base case plus inductive step gives it for all n in n
p m i prakaram anni n ki true

steps.why: The two proved statements are about n = 1 and about a step. Only the principle turns them into every n.
common_mistakes: Writing 'hence proved' without naming the principle.
steps.memory_tip: Name the principle in one sentence — it is worth a full mark.
